progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From c01: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl, 1 : 1; the chromate's 2 : 1 is the indicator's reaction; drop the rough titre; concordant titres within 0.10 mL; n = cV; divide by the aliquot; × 35.45 for g/L; seawater roughly 19 g/L chloride. From chem-m6-c12: rinse the burette with the solution it will hold; a volumetric flask makes a known dilution. From c02: mass → moles → ratio → target; extra mass reads high, lost solid reads low; constant mass; repeats keep a bias. From p02: a known value lets you judge accuracy; recovery. From skills-s07: accuracy is closeness to the true value; a systematic error pushes every trial the same way.
progression.startsWith: An unseen titration data set with a dilution. The video opens: Two ways to count ions you can't see: a titration that counts the silver it takes, and a precipitate you can weigh.
progression.stopsAfter: choosing concordant titres and the 1 : 1 Ag⁺ : Cl⁻ ratio; scaling an aliquot back through a dilution to the original sample in mol/L and g/L; excluding a gravimetric result for its stated cause; using a 1 : 3 formula ratio to find a percentage purity; explaining the direction of a titrant-dilution error and a lost-precipitate error; evaluating a claim built on the mean of two biased results.
progression.nextLesson: identifying cations (route chem-m8-c03a, "How do flame, precipitate and complex tests identify a cation?").

teaching.task: An exam gives you titres or precipitate masses, a method with something wrong in it, and a mole ratio waiting to trip you up. How do you decide which results to use, which ratio applies, how far to scale back, and which way an error pushes the answer?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why drop the rough titre: it is a guide, not a measurement (2b). Why 1 : 1: silver chloride's equation, not the indicator's (2b). Why ×10: the flask held ten aliquots (2c). Why divide by 10.00 mL: all those moles came from the original seawater (2c). Why exclude trial 3: its stated cause (not at constant mass) adds water and mass (3b). Why ÷ 3: each formula unit holds three sulfates (3c). Why 287% is wrong: a purity can't exceed 100% (3d). Why method 1 reads high: diluted titrant needs more volume, but the calculation uses the labelled concentration (4b). Why method 2 reads low: lost solid never reaches the balance (4c). Why the mean is not evidence: the errors are in opposite directions and only happen to cancel (4d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A titration counts the silver it takes and a precipitate can be weighed, and exam questions on both test the same few moves: use the right data, choose the right mole ratio, keep track of any dilution and say which way an error pushes the answer. Q1 (seawater diluted ten to two hundred and fifty millilitres, aliquots titrated with silver nitrate) drops the rough titre, averages the three concordant titres to 10.90 mL, takes the one to one silver chloride ratio rather than the chromate's two to one, then works moles of silver, the flask and the original ten millilitres to about 19.3 g/L, close to typical seawater; the classic slip stops at the aliquot. Q2 (aluminium sulfate purity by barium sulfate) excludes trial three because it was weighed after only one drying, not because it is different, uses the mean of the two constant-mass trials, and divides by three because each formula unit holds three sulfates, giving about 96%; the slip uses one to one and gets an impossible 287%. Q3 (a known chloride solution analysed by two faulty methods) explains why a water-rinsed burette dilutes the titrant and reads high and why precipitate lost through a torn paper reads low, calls both systematic, and shows that a mean near the known value is luck, not accuracy; the trap is trusting the average. A decision board closes: drop rough and faulty results with a reason, take the ratio from the precipitate, track every dilution and give each error's direction.
teaching.openingDecision: Two ways to count ions you can't see: a titration that counts the silver it takes, and a precipitate you can weigh. Exam questions on both test the same few moves. Use the right data, choose the right mole ratio, keep track of any dilution, and say which way an error pushes the answer. Here are three HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a): Q1's dilution volumes, the titrant concentration, all four titres and M(Cl); Q2's three masses with their drying notes and both molar masses; Q3's known value, both faults and both results, and the mean. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p58), as printed: "conduct investigations and/or process data involving: - gravimetric analysis - precipitation titrations" Practice and transfer only: first coverage stays with chem-m8-c01 (precipitation titrations), chem-m8-c02 and chem-m8-p02 (gravimetric analysis); G01 adds practice rows for processing data. starts at the route's "Interpret method and data for each quantitative analysis" and stops at its "Choose correct mole ratios and evaluate an error". Three questions, each with one trap: (1) a Mohr titration of diluted seawater: drop the rough titre, take the 1 : 1 ratio from the precipitate's equation, then scale back through the dilution to the original sample (trap: reporting the diluted solution's concentration); (2) a gravimetric purity check of aluminium sulfate: exclude a result for its stated cause, not its size, then use a 1 : 3 formula ratio (trap: using 1 : 1, which gives an impossible 287%); (3) the same known chloride solution measured by both methods, each with a stated fault: explain the direction of each error, then evaluate a claim that the mean of the two results shows accuracy (trap: trusting an average of two biased results). Not here: Mohr's indicator chemistry, the pH window and the blank (c01, recalled only where needed); the method steps and their reasons (c02, p02); acid-base titration (Module 6); back titration; ignition in a crucible.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G03 layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through each question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Titration with a dilution", "Gravimetric ratio", "Evaluate the errors"), hidden during each attempt because it names the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used. A check strip on the far left carries four rows, "which results to use?", "ratio from the precipitate?", "every dilution tracked?", "error: extra or lost, which way?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Colour key from c01 and c02: silver pale grey, chloride green, sulfate yellow-green, precipitate white; givens and units navy; the current answer bright; earlier lines dim; amber only for underlined givens. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; completed lines dim while the current line writes.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on as the Mohr flask and balance plates write side by side with a ratio chip between them; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its data table and demands; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given as it is used; the rough titre strikes out and a concordance bracket spans the three titres; the dilution ladder draws three stacked vessels and each stage line writes beside its rung, earlier lines dimming with their results kept; the outlier chip and constant mass chip write before the formula unit counter drops three barium sulfate tiles from one aluminium sulfate; the two-arrow error board draws with a dashed known line, the burette and torn filter thumbnails run their faults and each arrow points up or down; the mean marker writes near the line and slides below it when the tear grows; each question ends with its classic slip chip taking a red scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as a two-column board, each row lighting on its cue with its question badge; scene crossfade with settle.
